scenario: AITA for leaving to see my GF when my sister told me not to when she was "in charge"? | My mom is gone for a class thing in another state, and my dad is on a business trip so its just me, my sister and my brother all alone in the house. My sister is 18, I am 17 and my brother is 12, I don't know why but my parents still felt the need to leave my sister "in charge" while they were both gone. My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. On Sunday I was gonna go out with my GF for dinner, and my sister stopped me saying that I can't leave. When asked its cause "she said so", I laughed at that and I thought she was joking but she just kept looking and I knew it was a joke. I told her she can boss (little brother's name) around but she can't boss me, and I went out with my GF. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

This could be seen as **neglectful parenting** (*bal tashchit*—wasting potential, or failing to protect the family). 2. **Did you act with *midat hasidut* (piety) or *midat hadin* (justice)?** - Your sister’s reasoning ("she said so") was **arbitrary and unfair**. In Jewish ethics, authority must be **justified and reasonable**. If she had a valid reason (e.g., safety concerns, family rules), you might have had a stronger case to respect her. But since she was **abusing her position** (and laughing about it), your defiance could be seen as **standing up for justice** (*tzedek*). - However, **disrespecting a parent’s delegated authority** (even if unfair) can still be seen as *kibbud av va-eim* (honoring parents) being violated, unless the parent’s command is **unjust or harmful**. 3. **Did your mom handle it fairly?** - Grounding you for **disobeying your sister** (rather than addressing why your sister’s authority was misused) seems **unfair**. If your sister was truly in charge, she should have had **clear, reasonable rules**—not just "she said so." - If your mom had **addressed the issue properly** (e.g., "We trust you to make decisions, but not at the expense of fairness"), you might have had a stronger case for respecting her. But since she **punished you for standing up to an unfair system**, she may have been the one in the wrong. ### **What You Could Do Next:** 1. **Have a serious talk with your parents** when they return—**not as a confrontation, but as a discussion**: - *"I understand you trust [sister’s name], but she’s not always fair. Can we figure out a better system?"* - *"I didn’t want to fight, but I had to stand up for what was right."* 2. **Reinforce your relationship with your GF**—if this was a **personal freedom issue**, that’s valid. 3. **Work on your sister’s maturity**—if she’s abusing her "authority," you might need to **set boundaries with her too** (e.g., "If you’re going to be unfair, I won’t respect you"). ### **Bottom Line:** You **didn’t do anything wrong**—you **stood up for fairness**. The real issue is **your parents’ poor handling of the situation**, which is a **much bigger problem** than your defiance.
